title: What are JPA projections, how do interface, class/DTO, and dynamic projections differ, and how do they compare in performance?
keyPoints: Projections fetch only the columns you need instead of loading full managed entities, reducing data transfer and heap usage.
Interface projections declare getter methods and Spring builds a proxy; closed projections narrow the SQL, open projections load the full entity.
DTO/class projections use a JPQL constructor expression or a Java record and never enter the persistence context, making them the fastest option.
Dynamic projections accept a Class<T> parameter so one repository method returns different shapes at runtime.
Full entities are the slowest because every row enters the persistence context with a dirty-check snapshot.
Nested interface projections across associations can silently fire N+1 queries, so keep projections flat or use JOIN FETCH.

s1_definition.oneliner: Projections fetch only the columns you need as lightweight read models, far cheaper than loading full entities.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Projection** – a query result that returns only selected columns instead of the full entity, reducing data transfer, memory, and CPU.
- **Interface projection** – a plain Java interface with getter methods matching entity properties; Spring Data builds a proxy at runtime backed by only those columns.
- **Closed projection** – an interface projection where every getter maps directly to a property, allowing Hibernate to narrow the SQL SELECT to just those columns.
- **Open projection** – an interface projection using @Value SpEL expressions that can reference any property, forcing Hibernate to load the full entity first.
- **DTO/class projection** – a constructor expression in JPQL (`SELECT new ...`) or a Java record that produces an immutable, unmanaged object with no dirty-check overhead.
- **Dynamic projection** – a generic repository method with a `Class<T>` parameter so the caller picks the shape (interface, DTO, or full entity) at runtime.
s1_definition.analogy: Fetching a full entity is like National Bank of India pulling Rajesh's entire file, every page, photo, and history, just to read his balance. A projection is like asking only for a small index card with the two fields you actually need: name and balance. Interface projections are a card the clerk fills using a stencil (a proxy). DTO projections are a card you designed yourself with an exact slot for each field. Dynamic projections let you ask for different card layouts from the same request depending on what the caller wants.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Projection Type Comparison
  ============================================

  Full Entity                     Interface Projection
  +-----------+                   +------------------+
  | SELECT *  |                   | SELECT id, bal   |
  |     |     |                   |       |          |
  |     v     |                   |       v          |
  | Entity    |                   | JDK Proxy        |
  | + snapshot|                   | (no snapshot)    |
  | (managed) |                   | (not managed)    |
  +-----------+                   +------------------+

  DTO Projection                  Dynamic Projection
  +-----------+                   +------------------+
  | SELECT    |                   | <T> findBy(...)  |
  | new DTO(  |                   |       |          |
  |  id, bal) |                   |  Class<T> type   |
  |     |     |                   |       |          |
  |     v     |                   |   DTO? Entity?   |
  | Record    |                   |   Interface?     |
  | (plain)   |                   +------------------+
  +-----------+

  Performance Ranking (best to worst)
  ============================================
  1. DTO/Record projection   -- fewest columns, no proxy, no PC
  2. Closed interface proxy  -- fewest columns, small proxy cost
  3. Open interface proxy    -- loads FULL entity, then computes
  4. Full managed entity     -- all columns, snapshot, dirty check
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Projections let Rajesh return only the columns a read actually needs instead of loading full managed entities, which is a major win on the read-heavy dashboards at National Bank of India. There are three kinds: an interface projection is a plain Java interface with getters, and Spring builds a proxy backed by only those columns; a DTO projection uses a constructor expression or a record and produces an immutable object that never enters the persistence context; and a dynamic projection takes a Class parameter so one repository method can return different shapes at runtime.

On performance, loading full entities is the heaviest option because it selects every column, instantiates a managed entity, and registers it for dirty checking. Closed interface projections and DTO projections are the lightest because the SQL selects only the projected columns and the results are never managed. The one trap is the open interface projection using SpEL expressions, which loads the whole entity first and then computes, throwing away the benefit entirely.

The senior position Pankaj takes is that DTO projections are the default for read endpoints because they give the best performance, the strongest type safety, and an explicit API contract. Interface projections are a quick win for internal screens. Dynamic projections serve endpoints that must return both a summary and a full detail from one query. Full entities are reserved for methods that need to modify and save data.

Remember one sentence: DTO projections fetch the fewest columns and skip the persistence context entirely, making them the fastest read path in JPA.
